bullet_groups.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database's permission and rate limits, which became the Claude skill's main search tool

feedback.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database's permission and rate limits, which became the Claude skill's main search tool
feedback.problem: 'within the database's permission and rate limits' is ambiguous: 'permission limits' is not a standard concept, so the reader cannot tell whether the cache solved a throttling problem, an access-control problem, or both. It is also the most backend-shaped bullet in the internship but is placed last.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is exactly the bullet a backend interviewer will open with (cache design, invalidation, staleness of precomputed data), and the unclear constraint makes the motivation harder to restate.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 'permission limits' means here (e.g. read-only access, query quotas); how the precomputed tree is refreshed
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the constraint in plain words before the tech, e.g. 'Because the skill could only query PostgreSQL at a limited rate, precomputed ...'. Move this bullet to the top of Capital One.

feedback.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database's permission and rate limits, which became the Claude skill's main search tool
feedback.problem: The bullet leads with the mechanism ('Precomputed ... Redis-cached category tree') and the reason ('permission and rate limits') is a constraint a non-engineer can't picture. The payoff clause 'became the Claude skill's main search tool' depends on knowing what a 'Claude skill' is.
feedback.why_it_matters: I can't tell a hiring manager what problem this solved or who benefited without guessing, so I'll probably skip the bullet even though it's a real backend design choice.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the user or AI tool needed to look up, and what went wrong when it queried the database directly
feedback.suggested_direction: Open with the problem (the AI tool couldn't query the workflow database directly because of access and rate limits), then say what was built (a cached, category-organized index of popular workflows), then say it became the tool's main search path. Reuse the 'AI workflow generator' wording from the bullet above instead of 'Claude skill' so the two bullets read as one story.

feedback.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database’s permission and rate limits, which became the Claude skill’s main search tool
feedback.problem: Two problems. Mechanism: it is unclear how precomputing keeps lookups within 'permission' limits (rate limits make sense; permissions do not). Grammar: 'which became the Claude skill's main search tool' grammatically attaches to 'limits', not to the tree, and is an extra clause tacked on at the end.
feedback.why_it_matters: An interviewer will ask 'what permission limit?' and the candidate needs a crisp answer; a recruiter re-reads the sentence to find what 'which' refers to.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the permission constraint was (e.g., read-only replica access, query quota)
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the constraint plainly and put the 'main search tool' fact earlier so 'which' has an unambiguous referent, e.g. 'Built the Claude skill's main search tool by caching popular workflows from a 270K-row PostgreSQL table in Redis, so lookups stayed within the database's rate limits'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Co-built a topic-scoring research tool and deployed it to dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK to show Amazon Leo's public-policy staff which research topics are popular

feedback.bullet: Co-built a topic-scoring research tool and deployed it to dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK to show Amazon Leo's public-policy staff which research topics are popular
feedback.problem: The middle of the bullet is a tech list ('AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK') with no decision attached, and 'Co-built' plus 'deployed it to dev' leaves the candidate's own share and the tool's status unclear. The purpose arrives only at the end.
feedback.why_it_matters: A backend interviewer cannot tell whether the candidate wrote the CDK stacks and pipeline or the scoring logic, so the cloud evidence reads as name-dropping rather than ownership.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which part the candidate personally owned (infra as code, pipeline, scoring service)
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with what the tool does for the policy staff, then state the candidate's own piece, e.g. 'Wrote the AWS CDK stack and GitHub Actions pipeline that deploy ...'. Keep 'dev' — it is honest scoping.

feedback.bullet: Co-built a topic-scoring research tool and deployed it to dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK to show Amazon Leo's public-policy staff which research topics are popular
feedback.problem: 'deployed it to dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK' is a three-tool chain in the middle of the sentence, and 'to dev' is easy to miss, so the honest scoping (not production) gets lost.
feedback.why_it_matters: The purpose (policy staff seeing which topics are popular) is clear, but the infrastructure list reads as name-dropping instead of a decision.
feedback.suggested_direction: Keep 'deployed to a dev environment' in plain words and one infra term that shows ownership (e.g., 'with infrastructure as code'), and leave the rest to Skills.

feedback.bullet: Co-built a topic-scoring research tool and deployed it to dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK to show Amazon Leo’s public-policy staff which research topics are popular
feedback.problem: 'Co-built' leaves ownership unclear: what did Amar build versus the team? 'deployed it to dev' honestly admits it never reached production, but then the bullet's purpose ('to show ... staff') reads as if it is in use. 'on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK' is a tech dump of three tools with no engineering decision attached.
feedback.why_it_matters: Ambiguous ownership plus a list of deploy tools is a pattern screeners read as keyword padding; an interviewer will ask 'which part was yours?'.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which part Amar owned (the scoring logic, the infra, the deploy pipeline)
feedback.suggested_direction: Name Amar's piece first and keep only the tool that explains it (e.g., if he wrote the infra-as-code, say 'Wrote the AWS CDK stack and CI pipeline that deploy...'); let Skills carry the rest.

bullet_groups.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of Tortuga's Prisma ORM queries to reduce database load and latency for a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days

feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of Tortuga's Prisma ORM queries to reduce database load and latency for a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
feedback.problem: 'to reduce database load and latency' states intent, not result, and the only number (20,000+ visits) measures the product's traffic, not the cache. 'Tortuga' is an unexplained proper noun until 'class scheduler' arrives at the end.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader may attribute the 20,000 visits to the caching work, and an interviewer will ask what the cache actually changed; the bullet has no answer on the page.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: any observed change in DB load or response time after the cache, or what was cached and how it was invalidated
feedback.suggested_direction: Introduce the product first ('For Tortuga, a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, ...') so the traffic number reads as scale context, then the caching decision (what was cached / invalidation) if no measured result exists.

feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of Tortuga's Prisma ORM queries to reduce database load and latency for a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
feedback.problem: 'Tortuga' is never introduced, and a reader can't tell whether it's the product, a client, or a library. 'Prisma ORM queries' is jargon placed ahead of what the product is. The result is traffic (20,000+ visits), not the effect of the cache, so it's unclear what the caching achieved.
feedback.why_it_matters: The strongest part, a real product with 20,000+ visits, comes at the end after an unknown name.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: that Tortuga is the TerpLabs class scheduler
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the product first ('For Tortuga, TerpLabs' class scheduler (20,000+ visits in its first 30 days), added Redis caching in front of database queries to cut load and latency') and drop 'Prisma ORM' or move it to Skills, where Prisma already appears.

feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of Tortuga’s Prisma ORM queries to reduce database load and latency for a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
feedback.problem: The only number (20,000+ visits) measures the product's traffic, not the caching, so the bullet borrows a metric for work it does not measure. 'reduce database load and latency' ends at intent. 'Tortuga' is an unexplained proper noun and 'Tortuga's Prisma ORM queries' is a possessive noun stack.
feedback.why_it_matters: A skeptical reader sees the metric and the action are unrelated and starts doubting other numbers on the page.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what Tortuga is (the scheduler itself?) and whether the cache's effect was observed at all
feedback.suggested_direction: Introduce the product first and frame the traffic as context, e.g. 'Added a Redis cache in front of the database for Tortuga, a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, ...'; drop 'Prisma ORM' from the sentence.

bullet_groups.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp's candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick robot grasps that avoid hitting the table for a PhD-led project targeting ICLR

feedback.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp's candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick robot grasps that avoid hitting the table for a PhD-led project targeting ICLR
feedback.problem: Two trailing purpose clauses ('to help ... that avoid ... for a PhD-led project') make this a long chain; it is also the least backend-relevant item on the page.
feedback.why_it_matters: Minor for this audience; a backend reader will mostly skip it.
feedback.suggested_direction: Optional: split the purpose from the project context, or trim 'Built and prompt-tuned' to one verb. Fine to leave as is.

feedback.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp's candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick robot grasps that avoid hitting the table for a PhD-led project targeting ICLR
feedback.problem: 'AnyGrasp's candidate grasps' and 'in Open3D' come before the purpose, so the reader has to get through two unfamiliar names before learning it's about helping a robot choose where to grip. 'targeting ICLR' means nothing to most recruiters.
feedback.why_it_matters: I could restate it on the second read but skipped it on the skim. It's the only research role, so losing it hides the ML breadth that the intended profile claims.
feedback.suggested_direction: Reorder to goal, then method, then tools: helping a robot's AI model choose grips that avoid the table, by drawing candidate grips onto camera images, with AnyGrasp/Open3D named last or moved to Skills. 'targeting ICLR' can stay as the context at the end.

feedback.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp's candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick robot grasps that avoid hitting the table for a PhD-led project targeting ICLR
feedback.problem: Tacks an extra clause onto the end ('for a PhD-led project targeting ICLR'), which violates the one-clause structure rule. 'targeting ICLR' reads as a venue claim for unsubmitted work. There is no outcome: the bullet ends at intent ('to help ... pick').
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader skims 'ICLR' and assumes a paper, then feels misled when asked; and with no result, the bullet shows activity rather than a working system.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the overlay measurably changed grasp choices, or say it is in progress
feedback.suggested_direction: Cut the trailing project/venue clause (move 'PhD-led' context to the role line if needed) and end on what the pipeline does for the robot.

bullet_groups.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow tool as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation to make editing smoother, which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred

feedback.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow tool as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation to make editing smoother, which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred
feedback.problem: This is the first Capital One bullet a backend reader sees, and it is a desktop UI rebuild: React, TypeScript, Electron, React Flow and Jest are packed into one clause before the reader learns why. The backend-relevant Capital One work (the PostgreSQL/Redis lookup and the sub-skill split) sits below it.
feedback.why_it_matters: A backend interviewer skimming the second-strongest brand reads this as front-end work first and may pattern-match the internship as UI, even though the stronger backend bullet is two lines down.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: '90% ... preferred' implies preferred over the legacy tool; say so if true
feedback.suggested_direction: Reorder Capital One so the PostgreSQL/Redis bullet or the 65% generation-time bullet leads, and move this one to third. Within the bullet, lead with the tool and outcome and drop one of the stacked tech names (Electron or React Flow) to Skills if it does not explain the engineering.

feedback.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow tool as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation to make editing smoother, which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred
feedback.problem: Four technologies ('React and TypeScript Electron ... React Flow ... Jest-tested') sit between the action and the result, so the bullet runs to two dense lines before the reader reaches '90%'.
feedback.why_it_matters: It's a minor cost because the bullet is still clear. Trimming the tech list would get the reader to the payoff faster and make it sound less like a list.
feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the visual editor and the validation, which explain the design, and cut 'React and TypeScript' or 'Jest-tested' (both are already in Skills).

feedback.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow tool as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation to make editing smoother, which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred
feedback.problem: Parenthetical-style tech dump of five names (React, TypeScript, Electron, React Flow, Jest) in one stretch. 'make editing smoother' is vague. 'which 90% ... preferred' has no stated comparison (preferred over the legacy tool, presumably) and 'which' attaches to 'editing' rather than the app.
feedback.why_it_matters: The real story (a visual editor developers chose over the old tool) is buried behind keywords, and the 90% reads as unanchored.
feedback.suggested_direction: Keep Electron and the visual editor, cut the rest to Skills, and state the comparison, e.g. '...which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred over the old tool'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Built an EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift past a threshold

feedback.bullet: Built an EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift past a threshold
feedback.problem: Five jargon terms in a row ('EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check ... Amazon Bedrock classifier ... fine-tuning'), and 'its grades' could refer to the judge or to the classifier. The why (avoid retraining when nothing has changed) is implied, not stated.
feedback.why_it_matters: A recruiter can't restate this, and it reads like a stack of tools rather than a decision. It's the weakest of the three Amazon Leo bullets and the one I skipped on the skim.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whose grades drift (the classifier's ratings compared with the judge's?), and what retraining only on drift saves (cost, effort, or stability)
feedback.suggested_direction: Say the plain idea first, e.g. 'a scheduled check that uses a second model to spot when the production document classifier's ratings drift, so it is retrained only when needed', and move 'EventBridge' to Skills, where it already appears.

feedback.bullet: Built an EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift past a threshold
feedback.problem: Noun stacks: 'EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check' and 'production Amazon Bedrock classifier'. 'its grades' is ambiguous (the judge's grades or the classifier's?), and it is unclear whether the classifier or the check triggers fine-tuning. No result is given.
feedback.why_it_matters: A non-engineer cannot restate this, and an engineer has to parse it twice to work out the control loop, which is the interesting part.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whose grades drift and what the check compares against
feedback.suggested_direction: Say the loop in plain order: a scheduled job has a second LLM re-grade the classifier's outputs and kicks off fine-tuning only when the two disagree past a threshold. Keep 'Bedrock' or 'EventBridge', not both, in the sentence.

bullet_groups.bullet: Ran the full replay at 1.26M events/sec end-to-end on an order book that keeps std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map with an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1)

feedback.bullet: Ran the full replay at 1.26M events/sec end-to-end on an order book that keeps std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map with an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1)
feedback.problem: The second half ('std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map with an order-ID hash map ... O(1)') is pure code vocabulary. A non-engineer gets the throughput number and nothing else. The bullet also mixes two separate ideas: overall speed and how cancels are made fast.
feedback.why_it_matters: Recruiters and ATS/LLM screeners keep the 1.26M number but can't say why it was achievable. For an engineer reader it's the best design-choice bullet on the page, so the meaning is worth keeping.
feedback.suggested_direction: Put the design in words first ('orders kept in time-ordered queues per price, plus a lookup by order ID so cancels take constant time') and keep at most one concrete type name if it helps an engineer reader. Leave 1.26M events/sec as the result at the end.

feedback.bullet: Ran the full replay at 1.26M events/sec end-to-end on an order book that keeps std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map with an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1)
feedback.problem: Breaks the structure rule: 'Ran ... at 1.26M events/sec' is a measurement, not 'did X to accomplish Y', and the data-structure description is tacked on as a second idea. 'std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map with an order-ID hash map' is a three-container noun stack nobody says aloud. The throughput number has no baseline or hardware context, and std::list is a well-known cache-unfriendly choice that a performance-minded interviewer will challenge immediately.
feedback.why_it_matters: The page's main 'performance-sensitive systems' claim rests on a number the reader cannot judge and a design the reader may consider a weakness, so it can backfire in a systems interview.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 1.26M events/sec is compared against (single thread? what machine?) and why the cancel path mattered
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the design choice and its purpose in one sentence, then attach the throughput as the result, e.g. 'Kept a hash map from order ID to each resting order so cancels run in O(1), which let the full replay run at 1.26M events/sec'. Be ready to defend std::list or drop the container names.

bullet_groups.bullet: Building RAG meal suggestions for the official UMD app with SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes, which internal testers rated satisfactory for 93% of meals

feedback.bullet: Building RAG meal suggestions for the official UMD app with SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes, which internal testers rated satisfactory for 93% of meals
feedback.problem: 'to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes' is a stitched phrase that reads as if GPT-4o mini is being fed meals; the reader has to re-parse to understand that retrieval grounds the model's suggestions in real recipes.
feedback.why_it_matters: A non-engineer recruiter cannot restate this bullet in one pass, and the key design point (grounding to prevent made-up recipes) is lost.
feedback.suggested_direction: Rephrase the purpose in plain words, e.g. '... using SentenceBERT search over scraped recipes in ChromaDB so GPT-4o mini suggests real dishes, which ...'.

feedback.bullet: Building RAG meal suggestions for the official UMD app with SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes, which internal testers rated satisfactory for 93% of meals
feedback.problem: 'to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes' is a garden-path double object that readers stumble on. 'SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB' plus 'GPT-4o mini' is three named tools in one sentence. 'RAG meal suggestions' is a noun stack.
feedback.why_it_matters: A recruiter cannot restate what the feature does for a user; the purpose (grounding suggestions in real recipes) is hidden in the tech chain.
feedback.suggested_direction: Say the user-facing behavior first, then the mechanism once, e.g. 'Building meal suggestions for the official UMD app that retrieve real scraped recipes before the LLM answers, which internal testers rated satisfactory for 93% of meals'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Writing backtested Java capacity-planning logic that sets upper and lower bounds on the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching to balance availability against cost

feedback.bullet: Writing backtested Java capacity-planning logic that sets upper and lower bounds on the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching to balance availability against cost
feedback.problem: 'the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching' is a reduced relative clause that reads as a noun stack on first pass ('EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves').
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the top bullet on the page under the strongest brand; a one-pass stumble here costs attention in the first seconds of the skim.
feedback.suggested_direction: Add 'that' to break the noun stack: '... bounds on the EC2 capacity that Amazon Redshift reserves for patching, balancing availability against cost'.

feedback.bullet: Writing backtested Java capacity-planning logic that sets upper and lower bounds on the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching to balance availability against cost
feedback.problem: 'backtested Java capacity-planning logic' is a noun stack, and 'the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching' is a reduced relative clause that reads at first as 'Amazon Redshift reserves' (a noun).
feedback.why_it_matters: The top-of-page bullet at the strongest brand takes two reads to parse.
feedback.suggested_direction: Add 'that' and unstack, e.g. 'Writing Java logic, checked against historical data, that sets bounds on how much EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift holds back for patching, to balance availability against cost'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the engine’s event log to compare them on identical 2M-record workloads, which showed the B+ tree giving 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries for 27% more disk

feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the engine’s event log to compare them on identical 2M-record workloads, which showed the B+ tree giving 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries for 27% more disk
feedback.problem: Stacks three metrics in the tail clause. Reports only read-side results; LSM-trees exist to win on writes, so omitting write throughput looks cherry-picked to an informed reader. Why an append-heavy event log needs range queries is not explained.
feedback.why_it_matters: A storage-literate interviewer will immediately ask 'and writes?'; the bullet invites that question without the page answering it.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: the write-side comparison, or why reads were the deciding workload
feedback.suggested_direction: Keep one headline number and say which backend the engine kept and why, rather than listing three ratios.

bullet_groups.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda

feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
feedback.problem: Strong design-change bullet, but '6,000+ scraped research documents' has no time unit (total corpus vs. per day) and the 34% has no absolute scale (seconds vs. minutes).
feedback.why_it_matters: Backend interviewers will immediately ask the throughput and latency numbers; without scale the 34% is harder to anchor on the page.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: is 6,000+ a total or a rate; what the end-to-end latency was before/after if known
feedback.suggested_direction: If known, add the time unit or absolute latency in a few words; otherwise leave as is — the S3-to-Kinesis change is the right thing to emphasize.

bullet_groups.bullet: Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting a Claude skill into focused sub-skills that call Python search and validation tools instead of relying on open-ended model search

feedback.bullet: Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting a Claude skill into focused sub-skills that call Python search and validation tools instead of relying on open-ended model search
feedback.problem: Correct form, but 'instead of relying on open-ended model search' is a tacked-on contrast clause, and 'Claude skill' / 'sub-skills' is insider jargon a recruiter cannot restate.
feedback.why_it_matters: Minor length and plain-language cost on an otherwise strong, well-anchored bullet.
feedback.suggested_direction: Drop the 'instead of...' tail; the contrast is implied by 'focused sub-skills that call ... tools'.

page_feedback.problem: Is the strongest backend/cloud evidence visible first? Partly. AWS SDE Intern at the top is the right headline brand, but its single bullet is in progress with no result, and the next bullet a reader hits is a React/Electron UI rebuild. The clearest backend evidence (PostgreSQL/Redis lookup, S3-to-Kinesis/Lambda latency cut, EventBridge-scheduled eval) and the C++ matching engine sit in the lower two-thirds.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: In a 7-second skim a backend reader sees AWS + Capital One brands but may leave with 'front-end + LLM work' rather than 'systems/backend engineer' — the intended profile.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Reorder Capital One bullets so a backend bullet leads. Section order can stay (experience before projects is correct for these brands).

page_feedback.problem: Several bullets put the tool or mechanism before the purpose (Capital One bullet 3, Amazon Leo bullet 3, UMIACS, the third IEX bullet), so the page alternates between very clear bullets and bullets only an engineer can parse.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The profile is 'systems engineer who shipped real systems', and the clear bullets show that. The jargon-first bullets are where a non-technical screener stops reading, so the profile comes across only partly at recruiter level.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Apply the same order to every bullet: what problem or user, what was built, then the result. Keep the distinctive nouns (Kinesis, B+ tree, Redis) but put them after the plain-language purpose.

page_feedback.problem: The 'systems-oriented engineer' story only shows up at the bottom (IEX project). The top half is mostly LLM/workflow tooling (Claude skill, LLM-as-judge, RAG, VLM grasps), so a 7-second skim says 'AI-app builder', not 'backend/systems engineer'.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: For general backend roles, the strongest systems evidence (Kinesis latency cut, order-book replay accuracy) is not where the eye lands first.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Within each role, put the most backend/systems bullet first (e.g., the Kinesis latency bullet ahead of the topic-scoring tool bullet at Amazon Leo).

page_feedback.problem: Bolding is inconsistent. Some results are bold (90%, 65%, 93%, 50.9M, 12.8x, 1.26M events/sec), but equally strong numbers are not (34% latency, 20,000+ visits, 99,122 of 99,123). The bold also skews to the project and Capital One, not AWS.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: On a 7-second skim my eye jumps only to the bold numbers. The 99,122 of 99,123 match rate is the most impressive fact on the page and isn't bold, and the Amazon Leo section has no anchor at all.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Choose one bold anchor per role at most and apply it to the headline result of that role (e.g., the 34% latency cut for Amazon Leo, the fill-match figure for IEX), removing bold from secondary numbers.

page_feedback.problem: 'Amazon Leo' is used as a client name with no hint of what it is, and the employer line 'UMD App Development Contracting (Client: Amazon Leo)' makes it unclear whether this is a club, a university program, or paid work for Amazon.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Recruiters may misread this as a second Amazon job or dismiss it as a class project. Either way, the most cloud-heavy section of the page loses credibility on the skim.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: clarify: what UMD App Development Contracting is (a student contracting group? a university program?), in a few words on the title line, without adding new scope.

page_feedback.problem: Skills lists items no bullet backs up: 'fine-tuning and evaluation', PyTorch, OpenSearch, SQLAlchemy, API Gateway, CloudWatch, psutil.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: An interviewer who picks one of these and gets a thin answer starts discounting the whole list; 'fine-tuning' in particular overstates a bullet that only triggers fine-tuning.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Cut skills that cannot be defended for 5 minutes in an interview, or reword 'fine-tuning and evaluation' to match what was actually built (LLM evaluation).

page_feedback.problem: Three bullets end at intent with no outcome (AWS capacity bounds, UMIACS grasp pipeline, Bedrock judge check), and four use a trailing 'which ...' clause whose referent is grammatically ambiguous.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The repeated 'which' tail starts to read as a template, which hurts the human-voice impression across the page.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Vary the sentence shapes; use the 'cut <metric> N% by doing X' form where a real number exists and make sure each 'which' sits directly after the noun it describes.

page_feedback.problem: Skills lists REST APIs, API Gateway, Node.js, SQLAlchemy and OpenSearch, none of which appear in any bullet.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: An interviewer who probes a skill not evidenced anywhere may treat the list as padding, which slightly undercuts otherwise strong credibility.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep only skills the candidate can discuss from real work, or ensure the bullets that used them are recognizable (e.g. if the Amazon Leo tool exposes an API, say so).

page_feedback.problem: Proper nouns appear with no context: 'Tortuga', 'Amazon Leo', 'AnyGrasp', 'React Flow', 'IEX'.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Each one costs a non-specialist reader a beat, and several stacked in a bullet make it unrestatable.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Give each a 2-3 word gloss the first time it appears (e.g., 'Tortuga, a class scheduler'), or drop it where the generic noun does the job.

page_feedback.problem: Heading 'UMD App Development Contracting (Client: Amazon Leo)' puts a second Amazon name directly under the AWS internship.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A fast skimmer may briefly conflate the student contract with Amazon employment; the '(Contract)' title resolves it, so this is minor.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Fine as is; it is already honestly scoped.

page_feedback.problem: The AWS role, the biggest brand on the page and listed first, has one bullet that starts with 'Writing' and carries no outcome. This is accepted as a known gap, but the visual weight of the section is very light compared with Capital One.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: It's a minor point. The brand does the work on the skim, and the bullet is clear and honestly scoped.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: No change needed beyond keeping the bullet as clear as it is now. Don't pad it.

page_feedback.problem: What a backend interviewer would dig into: cache invalidation and freshness for the Redis category tree and the Tortuga cache; why Kinesis + Lambda over S3 staging (ordering, retries, cost) and what the 34% is measured on; how the LLM-as-judge threshold was chosen; the Redshift backtest methodology; and in the IEX project, single-thread vs. multi-thread at 1.26M events/sec, the 1 mismatched fill of 99,123, and why the B+ tree beat the LSM-tree on reads.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: These are the interview hooks the page creates; every one is a good conversation the candidate should be ready for.
